newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank deposit insurance assessment drops- FDIC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank deposit insurance assessment drops- FDIC.

text.p: With a healthy economy and a decline in bank failures, U.S. banks saw their assessments for deposit insurance drop by 97 percent last year, Federal Deposit Insurance Corp reported Tuesday.
But banks and savings and loans had to make special one-time payments of $4.5 billion to restore the savings industry's depleted deposit insurance fund.

Deposit insurance assessments for banks dropped to $73 million in 1996 from $2.9 billion in 1995 as the Bank Insurance Fund stood at a record $26.9 billion, up six percent from $25.5 billion a year earlier.
The bank fund had net earnings of $1.4 billion during the year, down from $3.6 billion in 1995 mainly due to the decline in assessments.
Operating expenses totaled $505 million, up from $471 million the previous year, the agency reported.
Banks and thrifts made payments totaling $5.2 billion into the savings industry fund, more than 85 percent in special one-time assessments, the agency reported.
The Savings Association Insurance Fund ended the year fully capitalized at $8.9 billion, also a record and up from $3.4 billion at the end of 1995.
Along with special one-time assessments on banks and thrifts, the fund earned $254 million on investments.
Operating expenses for 1996 totaled $63 million, up from $40 million the year before. Net income jumped to $5.5 billion from $1.4 billion in 1995.
The agency said the funds benefited from the small number of bank and savings and loan failures in 1996.

Five banks with total assets of $182 million failed in 1996, down from six banks with assets of $753 million the previous year. Losses from the failures totaled $43 million in 1996, down from $104 million in 1995.
One savings institution with assets of $35 million failed at a cost of $15 million, the agency said. No savings institutions had failed in 1995.
